exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Points of Intersection of Two Circles Where One Is Centered at the Origin

question.text: Find the polar coordinates for the intersection points of the circles $r=-2\sin\theta$ and $r=\sqrt{3},$ shown above.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r=-2\sin\theta \\ r=\sqrt{3} \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives

\begin{align} -2\sin\theta&=\sqrt{3}\\[5pt] \sin\theta&=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. \end{align}

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ .

Also, notice that $r=\sqrt{3}$ at both intersection points.

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\bigg(\sqrt{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\bigg)\quad$ and $\quad(r,\theta)=\bigg(\sqrt{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\bigg).$

question.text: The circles $r=1$ and $r=2\cos{\theta}$ intersect at points $A$ and $B,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates of the point $B?$
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$
\[ \begin{cases} r=2\cos\theta \\ r=1 \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for $\theta.$ This gives

\begin{align} 2\cos\theta &=1\\[5pt] \cos\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

Solving this equation in the interval $[0^\circ,\ \!360^\circ),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = 60^\circ$ and $\theta_2 = 300^\circ.$

Also, notice that $r=1$ at both intersection points.

Therefore, polar coordinates of the point $B$ are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\big(1, 300^\circ\big).$

question.text: The circles $r=-2\cos{\theta}$ and $r=1$ intersect for $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ at points $A$ and $B,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates $(r_A,\theta_A)$ and $(r_B,\theta_B)$ of the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively? Express the polar angles $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$ in radians.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r=-2\cos{\theta} \\[3pt] r=1 \end{cases} \]

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives

\begin{align} -2\cos{\theta}&=1 \\[5pt] \cos\theta&=-\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}.$

Also, notice that $r=1$ at both intersection points.

Therefore, the polar coordinates $(r_A,\theta_A)$ and $(r_B,\theta_B)$ of the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively, are

\[ (r_A,\theta_A)=\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{1}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{2\pi}{3}}\right),\quad (r_B,\theta_B)=\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{1}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{4\pi}{3}}\right). \]

question.text: The circles $r=2$ and $r=2\sqrt{2}\sin\theta$ intersect at points $A$ and $B,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates of the point $B?$
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$
\[ \begin{cases} r=2\sqrt{2}\sin\theta \\ r=2 \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solving for $\theta.$ This gives

Solving this equation in the interval $[0^\circ,\ \!360^\circ),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = 45^\circ$ and $\theta_2 = 135^\circ.$

Also, notice that $r=2$ at both intersection points.

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Points of Intersection Between a Circle and Another Curve

question.text: The circles $r=2\cos \theta $ and $r=-2\sin \theta $ intersect at points $O$ and $A,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates of the point $A?$
question.explanation:
First of all, we notice from the graph that the origin $O$ is an obvious first point of intersection.

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} 2\cos \theta&=-2\sin\theta\\[5pt] \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=-\dfrac{2}{{2}}\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=-1 \end{align}

This gives us the solution $\theta =315^\circ$ in the $4$th quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=2\cos\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} r &=2\cos\left(315^{\circ}\right)\\[5pt] &=2\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\\[5pt] &=\sqrt2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\left(\sqrt2, 315^{\circ}\right).$

example.title: Finding the Points of Intersection Between a Circle and Another Curve

question.text: The circles $r=3\sin\theta$ and $r=3\cos\theta$ intersect at points $O$ and $A,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ of the point $A?$ Express the polar angle $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ in radians.
question.explanation:
First of all, we notice from the graph that the origin $O$ is an obvious first point of intersection.

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} 3\cos\theta&=3\sin\theta\\[5pt] \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=1\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=1 \end{align}

This gives us the solution $\theta =\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the $1$st quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=3\sin\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} r&=3\sin\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\bigg)\\[5pt] &=3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, polar coordinates of the point $A$ are

\[ (r,\theta) = \left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\right).\]

question.explanation:

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \cos\theta&=\sin\theta\\[5pt] \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=1\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=1 \end{align}

This gives us the solution $\theta =\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the $1$st quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=\sin\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} r&=\sin\bigg(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\bigg)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Points of Intersection Between a Circle and Another Curve

question.text: The circles $r=3\cos \theta $ and $r=\sqrt{3}\sin \theta $ intersect at points $O$ and $A,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates of the point $A?$
question.explanation:
First of all, we notice from the graph that the origin $O$ is an obvious first point of intersection.

To find the second point of intersection, we set the equations of the curves equal to each other and solve for $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \sqrt{3}\sin \theta&=3\cos(\theta)\\[5pt] \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=\sqrt{3} \end{align}

This gives us the solution $\theta =60^\circ$ in the $1$st quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=3\cos\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of the point $A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} r &=3\cos\left(60^{\circ}\right)\\[5pt] &=3\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 60^{\circ}\right).$

question.text: The curves $r=\sqrt{3}-2\sin \theta$ and $r= -4 \sin \theta$ intersect for $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ at points $A$ and $B,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates $(r_A,\theta_A)$ and $(r_B,\theta_B)$ of the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively? Express the polar angles $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$ in radians.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$
\[ \begin{cases} r = -4 \sin \theta \\[2pt] r = \sqrt{3}-2\sin \theta \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives \[ \eqalign{ -4 \sin \theta & = \sqrt{3}-2\sin \theta \\[5pt] -2 \sin \theta & = \sqrt{3} \\[5pt] \sin \theta & = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\, . } \] Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}.$

Now, we use the equation $ r = -4 \sin \theta$ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points: \[ \eqalign{ r_1 & =-4 \sin \left(\dfrac {4\pi} 3\right) = -4\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)= 2\sqrt{3} \\[5pt] r_2 & =-4 \sin \left(\dfrac {5\pi} 3 \right) = -4\!\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)= 2\sqrt{3} } \] Therefore, the polar coordinates $(r_A,\theta_A)$ and $(r_B,\theta_B)$ of the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively, are \[ (r_A,\theta_A)=\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{2\sqrt{3}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{4\pi}{3}}\right),\quad (r_B,\theta_B)=\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{2\sqrt{3}}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{5\pi}{3}}\right). \]

question.text: The curves $r = 2-3\cos \theta$ and $ r =  -7\cos \theta$ for $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$ intersect at a single point in the third quadrant. Determine the polar coordinates of this point. Express the polar angle $\theta$ in radians.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r = 2-3\cos \theta \\ r = -7 \cos \theta \end{cases} \]

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives \[ \eqalign{ 2-3\cos \theta & = -7\cos \theta \\[5pt] 2 & = -4\cos\theta \\[5pt] \cos \theta & = -\dfrac {1} {2}\, . } \]

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = \dfrac {2\pi}{3}$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac {4\pi}{3}.$

Therefore, the $\theta$-coordinate of the point that we're interested in is $\theta = \dfrac {4\pi}{3},$ since it lies in the third quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $ r = -7\cos \theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of our point:

\[ r = -7\cos \left(\dfrac {4\pi} {3} \right) = \dfrac{7}{2}. \]

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the desired intersection point are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{7}{2}},\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{4\pi}{3}}\right).$

question.text: Find the polar coordinates of the intersection points of the polar curves $r =2-2\sin \theta $ and $ r = 1,$ shown above.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \eqalign{ \quad r & =2-2\sin \theta \\ \quad r& = 1 } \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives \[ \eqalign{ 2-2\sin \theta & = 1\\[5pt] 2\sin \theta & = 1 \\[5pt] \sin \theta & = \dfrac 1 2 . \\ } \]

Solving this equation in the interval $[0^\circ,360^\circ),$ we obtain $\theta_1 =30^{\circ}$ and $\theta_2 = 150^\circ.$

Notice that we must have $r=1$ for any point that lies on both curves.

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\left(1, 30^{\circ}\right)\quad $ and $\quad (r,\theta)= \left(1, 150^{\circ}\right).$

example.title: Finding the Points of Intersection of a Limaçon and Another Curve

question.text: Find the polar coordinates of the intersection points of the polar curves $r =3-2\sin \theta $ and $ r = 4+3\sin \theta,$ shown above. Round your answers to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r = 3-2\sin \theta \\ r = 4+3\sin \theta \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives

\[ \eqalign{ 3-2\sin \theta & = 4+3\sin \theta\\[5pt] 5\sin \theta & = -1 \\[5pt] \sin \theta & = -\dfrac 1 5 . } \]

Solving this equation in the interval $\left[0^\circ,360^\circ\right),$ we obtain $\theta_1 \approx 191.5^{\circ}$ and $\theta_2 \approx 348.5,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place.

Now, we use the equation $r =4 + 3\sin\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points:

\[ \eqalign{ r_1 & =4 + 3\sin \theta_1 =4 +3\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}5\right)= \dfrac{17}{5} =3.4\\[5pt] r_2 & =4 + 3\cos \theta_2 =4 +3\cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}5\right)= \dfrac{17}{5} =3.4 } \]

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta) \approx \big(3.4, 191.5^\circ \big) \quad$ and $\quad (r,\theta) \approx \big(3.4, 348.5^\circ\big).$

example.title: Finding the Points of Intersection of a Limaçon and Another Curve

question.text: The polar curves $r =5-4\sin \theta $ and $ r = 1+4\sin \theta$ intersect  for $\theta\in [0^\circ, 360^\circ)$ at points $A$ and $B,$ as shown above. What are the polar coordinates $(r_A,\theta_A)$ and $(r_B,\theta_B)$ of the points $A$ and $B,$ respectively? Express the polar angles $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$ in degrees.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r = 5-4\sin \theta \\[5pt] r = 1+4\sin \theta \end{cases} \] We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives

\[ \eqalign{ 5-4\sin \theta & = 1+4\sin \theta\\[5pt] 8\sin \theta & = 4 \\[5pt] \sin \theta & = \dfrac12\, . } \]

Solving this equation in the interval $\left[0^\circ,360^\circ\right),$ we obtain $\theta_1 =30^\circ$ and $\theta_2 =150^\circ.$

Now, we use the equation $r = 1+4\sin\theta$ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points:

\[ \eqalign{ r_1 & = 1 + 4\sin \theta_1 = 1 + 4\cdot \dfrac12= 3\\[5pt] r_2 & = 1 + 4\sin \theta_2 = 1 + 4\cdot \dfrac12= 3 } \]

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

\[ (r_A,\theta_A) = \left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{3}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{30} ^\circ\right) \quad\text{and } (r_B,\theta_B) = \left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{3}, \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{150}^\circ\right). \]

example.title: Finding the Points of Intersection of a Limaçon and Another Curve

question.text: The curves $r =2-3\sin \theta $ and $ r = \sin \theta$ for $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$ intersect at a single point in the second quadrant. Determine the polar coordinates of this point.
question.explanation:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{cases} r =2-3 \sin \theta \\ r =\sin \theta \end{cases} \]

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta.$ This gives \[ \eqalign{ 2-3 \sin \theta & = \sin \theta \\[5pt] 4 \sin \theta & = 2 \\[5pt] \sin \theta & = \dfrac 1 2 . } \]

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi),$ we obtain $\theta_1 = \dfrac {\pi}{6}$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac {5\pi}{6}.$

Therefore, the $\theta$-coordinate of the point that we're interested in is $\theta = \dfrac {5\pi}{6},$ since it lies in the second quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $ r = \sin \theta$ to find the $r$-coordinate of our point:

\[ r = \sin \left(\dfrac {5\pi} {6} \right) =\dfrac 1 2 \]

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the desired intersection point are

$\qquad$ $(r,\theta)=\bigg(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\bigg).$
